evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析；形義源流通解；甲骨、金文、戰國用例
evidence.text: The entry presents three proposals for the early form: 六 and 入 may have been the same graph, with later strokes differentiating a numeral use; it may depict a shelter and be an earlier graph for 廬; or it may have been a conventional counting mark. It says Xu Shen’s 說文 explanation uses 易 numerology and likely does not recover the graph’s original meaning. It cites oracle-bone uses as a cardinal in 合集 32320 (燎六羊) and ordinal in 合集 7775 (六月), and later bronze and Warring States numeral uses. These attestations establish numeral use by the late Shang material represented by the cited oracle-bone records; they do not establish the relative chronology of the graphic proposals.
evidence.kind: character-specific paleographic dictionary and cited primary attestations
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：六

evidence.source: Kotobank, 精選版 日本国語大辞典 and 普及版 字通
evidence.field: 六: 字形, 字音, 語義, 初出実例
evidence.text: 字通 endorses the shelter interpretation, describing oracle-bone and bronze forms as a small tent or shelter and the numeral as a phonetic loan, while noting the 說文 explanation and that its seal form is not the graph’s initial form. The same page reports the competing possibility, in its Japanese dictionary material, that the shelter is a pictographic form related to 廬. Separately, it records Japanese numeral uses and gives dated examples: ろく in 万葉集 (late 8th century), むゆ in 日本書紀 (720, as a reading in the cited manuscript tradition), and a counting sequence in 年中行事秘抄 (late 12th century). These are Japanese lexical records, not dates for the Chinese graph’s origin.
evidence.kind: historical dictionary with dated Japanese attestations and a paleographic account
evidence.title: 六（読み）ロク - コトバンク

evidence.source: 字源考釋 - 六, 香港教育城相關字源資源
evidence.text: The page labels images as oracle-bone, bronze, seal, and standard forms and explicitly interprets the first three as a front view of a shelter, said to be the original graph for 廬, later borrowed for the numeral 六. The accessible text does not provide a dating argument or pronunciation evidence for the supposed shelter-name, and the glyph images were not visually inspected in this research.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 - 六

evidence.field: Old Chinese reconstruction table: 六 and 廬 entries
evidence.text: In the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese system, 六 is listed with Mandarin liù, Middle Chinese transcription ljuwk, Old Chinese *k.ruk, gloss ‘six’; 廬 is listed with Mandarin lú, Middle Chinese ljo, Old Chinese *[r]a, gloss ‘hut; inn; to lodge’. The authors explain that their Middle Chinese transcription is a representation of source pronunciation rather than a reconstruction, and that bracketed segments mark uncertainty. The reconstructed forms differ substantially; their table alone does not substantiate a sound-based loan from the word 廬 to the numeral 六. The word *[r]a supports a historical pronunciation proposal for 廬, but cannot establish that an object depicted by 六 was actually named 廬.
evidence.kind: primary reconstruction dataset; Oxford University Press authors’ published table
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (13 September 2014)

evidence.text: The table identifies itself as Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction version 1.1, dated 13 September 2014. It defines the Middle Chinese column as a convenient transcription based on historical sources, not a reconstruction; Old Chinese forms are system-specific reconstructions and bracket notation marks uncertainty. These qualifications apply to the listed forms *k.ruk and *[r]a.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (13 September 2014)

evidence.text: This secondary character page calls 六’s origin unclear and summarizes the 入 differentiation and hut/L廬 proposals. It gives oracle script (~1250–1000 BC), early Western Zhou bronze (~1000 BC), Shuowen seal (~100 AD), and Eastern Han clerical forms, but these dates are labels for example script forms, not proof that the numeral meaning arose at a particular date. Its historical pronunciation table gives *k.ruk, ljuwk, liù; the primary Baxter–Sagart table was checked independently for that notation.
evidence.title: 六 - Dong Chinese dictionary

search_audit.outcome: Opened the shelter interpretation page and Baxter–Sagart table; confirmed both 六 and 廬 entries and their readings. Oxford book page was opened for publication context. The compared Baxter–Sagart reconstructions do not supply independent support for the proposed 廬-to-six loan.

gaps: The competing early graphic interpretations remain unresolved: the available character-specific source reports the 入-related differentiation account, the shelter/L廬 account, and a numeral-mark possibility, but no consulted primary inscription image or specialist argument settles them.

The shelter-name hypothesis is not phonologically established as a borrowing account: the original referent and its name/pronunciation are not independently recovered. Baxter–Sagart gives 廬 *[r]a versus 六 *k.ruk, which does not by itself support a sound match; these are system-specific reconstructions, not proof against every other account.

The CUHK page cites oracle-bone records 合集 32320 and 7775 and reports cardinal and ordinal functions, but the cited original inscriptions were not opened; no exact dated inscription photographs or earliest semantic transition were verified. Do not infer numeral chronology from later dictionary glosses.

The graph’s proposed stages after oracle and bronze forms were not independently inspected visually. Dong Chinese labels seal and clerical exemplars, while CUHK supplies later Warring States attestations, but this audit does not establish each graphic transformation or identify a specific corruption.

The official Unicode Unihan URL for U+516D was attempted twice and remained inaccessible. Local kMandarin rows report liù, but the required official character-specific click-through could not be verified.

No local kMandarin row for 廬 was checked in this run; its historical and modern readings above come from the externally opened Baxter–Sagart PDF. Modern Mandarin readings are metadata, not evidence for an ancient sound relation.
